How a page earns a reader

A reader decides in seconds. The page either shows what it is about or it does not. Short sentences help. So does a heading that says something.

What gets measured

Sentence length, word length and vocabulary rarity are the levers every classic formula pulls. None of them measure whether the argument is any good, and that limit is worth stating out loud.

  • Line length, measured on the rendered page
  • Contrast, resolved through the background stack

Why the rendered page matters

A formula reads the words and stops there. It never sees the twelve pixel caption, the line that runs to a hundred and forty characters, or the grey that sits at two and a half to one against white. Those are the things a reader actually feels, and they are only visible once the page is rendered in a browser at a real width.

So the measurement happens twice. The text is pulled out of the markup and scored for sentence length, word rarity and voice. Then the same page is loaded at fourteen hundred pixels and again at three hundred and ninety, and the type is read back from the computed styles: size, leading, measure, and the contrast of every block against the background it truly sits on.

Neither half is sufficient alone. Clear prose set in grey nine pixel type is unreadable, and a beautiful column of text that says nothing is a waste of the reader's afternoon. The score here is a weighted mean of both, minus a penalty for every concrete defect that was found.
